RagShortTexts: The economic sustenance of Angles in 374 AD relied upon extensive agrarian estates, pastoral herds, and strategic mineral extraction.
Anchored around commercial hubs near Southern Jutland (Angeln), merchant caravans traded valuable bullion, grain, wine, and exotic raw goods.
Advanced weapon smithies and metallurgical workshops provided the industrial backbone necessary to equip large armies in the field.

Variants.Content: Underpinning the immense martial demands of Angles was an agrarian and mercantile economic system rooted in rural estates and municipal workshops. Across fertile valleys and pastures, countless tenant farmers and laborers produced wheat harvests, vintage wines, cured pelts, and high-grade iron ingots destined for storehouses. Within thriving market plazas around Southern Jutland (Angeln), cosmopolitan merchants converged to barter gold coinage, imported silks, fine armaments, and livestock. Imperial or royal customs officials maintained toll gates, extracting heavy excise duties from freight wagons. Yet the system faced constant vulnerability from harvest failures and trade route disruptions, compelling rulers to enforce grain requisitions to sustain armies in the field.

Wet fen paths in the Angeln marshes swallow the wagon wheels, and the cooks argue over whether the salt pork is still safe to boil. Spearmen carry their share of the grain on their backs and count the days until the next issue. Few men in the ranks own silver, so most buy a replacement strap or whetstone on credit against the promise of loot.

Our bailiff in Anglia writes in hard ink: the tenth sheaf from the coastal farms is short, and the herring barrels spoiled before they reached the Jutland quay. Ask the sea merchants whether they will advance silver against next year's crop. Discretion matters more than price, since a rival lord who learns our granaries are empty will press his claims.
